extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and practitioners interested in 19th-century American newspaper history and newspaper_format/content practices
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts mid‑19th‑century standards for newspaper format, editorial practice, advertising, distribution, and legal/ethical limits as described in a historical survey of American newspapers (1833–1860). Useful for understanding how papers were produced, judged, and managed in that period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Page size and issue length
rubrics_metrics.description: Page size, number of columns, and number of pages in an issue (e.g., Herald page carried six columns in 1840 and measured 15 x 22 inches; eight-page papers became common among Times, Herald, Tribune; country weeklies generally had four pages).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smaller penny papers began with small pages and grew as business expanded. Page size and issue length signaled a paper's class and capacity to carry content and advertising.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial page as a department / composition
rubrics_metrics.description: The editorial page was a distinct department, typically containing one to four columns of editorials, often preceded by a column summary of important news and sharing space with a Washington letter, book reviews and other material; news on this page moved toward the 'informative editorial.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect a mixture of opinion, summarizing material, and non-news features; the page should blend commentary with informative elements rather than pure reportage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial literary quality and range
rubrics_metrics.description: Editorial pages should 'discuss in an adequate literary style a large variety of contemporary topics'—political, social, economic, and literary—and 'represent wide information' and 'hold to high aims' (Greeley/Tribune model).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Produced by skilled writers under editorial supervision; breadth of subject matter and literary quality are hallmarks of a modern editorial page.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial tone, fairness, and paragraphing
rubrics_metrics.description: Tone and style are evaluative criteria: e.g., New York Herald editorials distinguished by short paragraphs, often flippant and cynical; the Times characterized by 'unusual fairness'; Evening Post militant and eloquent advocate of particular causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tone can range from cynical/sardonic to fair and balanced; paragraph length and rhetorical posture (pungent short paragraphs vs. longer 'leaders') are indicators of editorial approach and seriousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial topical focus for country weeklies
rubrics_metrics.description: Country weeklies commonly made politics their main editorial topic; editors in smaller towns were expected to discuss national politics at length.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Local papers were judged by their political commentary and engagement with national issues, analogous to a civic duty.

rubrics_metrics.name: News selection: national significance and continuing stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Papers were expected to cover the great continuing national stories of the era—national politics, wars (e.g., Mexican War), and major economic events (e.g., gold rush)—and to treat chief breaks and campaigns prominently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: News judgment favored nationally significant, continuing narratives and key campaign/war developments; coverage choices signaled editorial priorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensationalism / 'pepper‑pot' news concept
rubrics_metrics.description: Penny papers exploited murder sensations and other lurid stories under a 'pepper-pot' news concept; some stories were 'overplayed' by cheap papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sensational coverage increased sales but risked criticism for excess; overemphasis on lurid detail is an anti-pattern compared with measured reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of extras and practical information for big events
rubrics_metrics.description: Issuing extras and specialized editions (e.g., Bennett's California Herald with maps, official reports, and data on how to reach gold fields) for major news events was a practice to amplify coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extras and practical guidance (maps, travel data) were judged useful in meeting readers' informational needs and commercial demand during big stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertising placement / front‑page advertising policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Front pages were commonly filled with advertising until the 1850s; leading publishers of eight‑page papers banished advertising from their front pages as a marker of status, though some four‑page papers continued to give prime position to advertisers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Front‑page advertising or its absence signaled editorial standing; moving ads off front pages was considered a quality/formal improvement by some publishers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertising typography and layout ('agate rule')
rubrics_metrics.description: There was little display advertising; the usual ad type-size was agate in single‑column width. Large papers adopted an 'agate rule' (single-column agate, no stock-cuts or two‑line initials); double-column or display measures were often abandoned as wasteful and unfair to small advertisers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consistent small-type single-column ads favored economy and fairness; attempts at display were often judged inefficient or inequitable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertisement rotation and freshness policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Policies governing ad duration and freshness—Bennett ordered ads not accepted for more than two weeks and later required daily change of copy, advertising with the slogan 'Advertisements Renewed Every Day.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frequent renewal of ad copy was promoted to maintain the 'fresh, newsy quality' of advertising pages. Standing/unchanged ads were seen as reducing value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertising creativity and promotional tactics
rubrics_metrics.description: Tactics to overcome monotony included logotype compositions (forming words into street numbers), iteration copy (repeating a short ad to fill a column), and serial promotions (printing a chapter then directing readers to buy another weekly).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Creative typographic or copy devices were accepted methods to draw attention under restrictive ad formats; they served circulation and promotional aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertising rates and payment practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Rates were in confusion—annual contracts ($40/year) and per‑square pricing (penny papers starting at fifty cents a square) varied; rules like advance payment (initiated by the New York Sun) developed; unpaid accounts and 'payment in kind' were common problems; agencies negotiated rates and took commissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rate structures and payment policies influenced who advertised where and could affect editorial independence and paper solvency; advertisers and agents shaped the marketplace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial stance on soliciting and censoring advertisements
rubrics_metrics.description: Many publishers refused to solicit ads but also refused to censor advertisers' language beyond indecency; Greeley's and Boston Daily Times' positions: editors not responsible for advertisers' style (if decent) and caveat emptor for product claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Papers generally accepted paid advertisements unless indecent; they regarded policing advertisers' product claims as the reader's responsibility, not the editor's—an explicit editorial policy posture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selective ad acceptance as a quality control
rubrics_metrics.description: Some papers enforced selective ad acceptance, excluding certain classes (e.g., 'Advertisements of certain classes of Medicines, Doctors, Books, &c.' refused by the Times in 1852); high‑class papers often excluded patent‑medicine advertising altogether.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refusing objectionable or low‑quality ad classes was used as an editorial quality signal and a reputational safeguard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distribution practices and postal policy impact
rubrics_metrics.description: Delivery mechanisms (local carriers vs. postoffice), exchanges of papers between publishers (gratis since 1792), and postoffice acts (free county delivery, postage cuts, prepaid discounts) materially affected circulation and distribution strategies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Postal rules and delivery arrangements determined reach and economic viability; publishers adapted subscription/pricing and mailing practices accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resistance to postal censorship and legal limits on distribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Attempts were made to empower the Postoffice to refuse circulation of 'obnoxious papers' to Southern states; bills and proposals arose but faced constitutional objections; state laws in the South forbade 'incendiary publications.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal/political attempts to censor by controlling postal distribution were significant threats to press freedom; resistance and legislative defeat of such measures were part of the normative framework protecting distribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Libel law and legal constraints on press content
rubrics_metrics.description: Libel suits were a limitation on press freedom; during the period suits declined as states liberalized laws; notable suits (e.g., Cooper's suits) led to the principle that truth is admissible as a defense in civil libel actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal exposure for libel shaped editorial caution; the availability of truth as a defense was an important protection for newspapers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporter accreditation, access, and parliamentary reporting rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Congressional accreditation practices constrained reporter access: the House and Senate limited reporters (e.g., Senate restricted to local papers until 1846), with progressively more systematic and fair accrediting by 1860.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Access rules influenced coverage quality and national reporting; changes in accreditation reflected evolving norms about national press access to legislative proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional conduct, civility, and avoidance of personal abuse
rubrics_metrics.description: Editorial billingsgate and violent personal attacks declined; editors in some locales resolved 'to abstain from all disrespectful personal allusions or epithets toward each other'; duels and physical violence were noted as extreme anti‑patterns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Civility and restraint in personal abuse became a professional norm; failure to observe this could lead to reputational harm and physical reprisals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press integrity and responsiveness to criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Contemporary critics (Cooper, Dickens, Wilmer) accused the press of corruption, slander, and undue influence; such criticisms served as yardsticks for evaluating press integrity and the 'public will' to maintain freedom despite unpopular views.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A paper's susceptibility to corrupt influence or reliance on ribald slander was a negative mark; responsiveness to public critique and maintenance of editorial integrity were implicit standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion of popular culture and human-interest topics
rubrics_metrics.description: Papers devoted space to sports (horse racing, cricket, prizefighting), popular 'dementias' (phrenology, spiritualism), celebrity visits, and sensational movements (Millerism); these topics furnished circulation and reader interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balancing popular, sensational, and serious public‑affairs coverage was a practical editorial criterion—broad appeal could boost circulation, but overemphasis risked undermining seriousness.
